story_text.value:
tinytowns makes up new town names in the style of real ones. It learned the letter patterns of 128,435 real place names: it was trained to guess the next letter of a place name as well as it can. It does not know which places exist, so most names it writes are new.

Applications: - Make names for towns in games and on maps. - Make test data with place names that are not real. - Tell if a word looks like a place name. For example, it could find asdfgh in a city field.

title.value: Show HN: Tinytowns, a small model to generate realistic sounding town names

story_text.value:
12 years ago today (Oct 22, 2014), Google released Inbox by Gmail™, definitively solving email UX. Even now, 7 years after Google made the objectively incorrect decision to shut it down, almost nothing has come close to Inbox's elegant way of visualizing and organizing emails.

(The best attempt by far was a cloud email service called Shortwave, which was at least initially intended as a true spiritual successor to Inbox. Sadly, even that project ultimately strayed too far from the Inbox UX, implementing a non-optional 2-pane view that did away with one of Inbox’s best UX concepts.)

Given this constant stream of false starts and betrayals, I wanted to build something that looked and worked more or less exactly like the original Inbox, but was fully local and could work with any email account. Something that, once you had it on your computer, wouldn’t suddenly vanish or change because the creator lost interest or suddenly got a different idea about how your email should look!

Since it's just a Thunderbird extension, NeoInbox works with any email account, and runs completely locally. It also includes all your favorite classic Google Inbox features like a unified mail stream, bundling, trip detection, reminders, and more! Give it a try!

title.value: Show HN: NeoInbox, a recreation of Google Inbox as a Thunderbird extension

story_text.value:
If you use AI to create images and videos, you most likely use Higgsfield or similar subscription tools.

I did too. But I had 3 main issues with it:

The markup is super high. So if the model provider charges x, higgsfield charges a markup of + 50% on top.

Credits I did not use would expire every month....EVEN THOUGH I PAID FOR IT

And I had to switch between Claude and Higgsfield constantly...copy pasting prompts and all

So I built a free open source repo of creative production skills for AI agents.

So basically, you just install this skill package in Claude (or any agent you use) and say "Create a summer sale UGC video for my product". And it handles the rest. You obviously stay in control all along.

And:

You can use your own API keys...which adds ZERO markup on the model provider costs

There is no subscription. You only pay for what you use and nothing EXPIRES

And no more switching between tools and no more copy pasting

We are releasing the skills in batches. The first batch that can research the market, create ugc videos, product videos, product photoshoots, etc. is already live here: https://github.com/SupercmoHQ/superCMO-skills

title.value: Show HN: Open-source Claude skills to replace Higgsfield

story_text.value:
What pawmc is (from the blog post):

It’s an LLM chat app with minimal system prompt and no tools/web-search by design. It stores most important context across your conversations in isolated buckets, called “diaries” and “topics”. This means that when you start a conversation in { diary: personal, topic: books }, the AI receives your first message along with summaries of that diary and that topic. It’s close in concept to Karpathy’s LLM Wiki, but simpler, easier to wrap your head around and maintain — no extra tooling and no different types of documents: it’s just your conversations as the source of truth and the summaries of topics and diaries as the “wiki”

Post links a hosted demo with a scripted walkthrough of a typical flow, no LLM.

And here is the repo: https://github.com/kol3x/pawmc

title.value: Show HN: Pawmc a.k.a. talking diary, an LLM chat with compartmentalised memory

story_text.value:
Hello. I built a blogging platform on my own over two years.

I like running my blog, but I couldn't find a blogging platform I really liked.

First. I thought a blog had to be really lightweight. Fortunately, after a lot of effort, I was able to achieve satisfactory results. (99 to 100 score)

Here is a sample blog: https://bloffy.bloffy.blog/en

You can check it with PageSpeed Insights: https://pagespeed.web.dev/analysis?url=https://bloffy.bloffy...

SEO score of the sample blog is low because I blocked it from search engine indexing (noindex).

Second. I think bloggers should have control over their own blog. The blogging platforms I used had several problems.

Unnecessary JavaScript chunks. Ads that the platform inserted into my blog, not my own ads. Cannot manage multiple blogs. An editor that makes it hard to write semantic markup. Limited customization options. I was dissatisfied with the difficulty of placing my own ads.

And to solve this, I spent quite a long time researching and developing it on my own, and finally created it. I'm glad to share this launch with HN. I would appreciate any criticism, feedback, and interest.

title.value: Show HN: I built a Markdown and raw HTML blog platform scoring 99 on PageSpeed
